Upstate NYDBER 2026: Conference Report & Consensus-Building Summary

Cornell University · June 11–12, 2026

August 07, 2026

Welcome

Upstate NYDBER 2026 brought together Discipline-Based Education Research (DBER) scholars — across Physics (PER), Biology (BER), Engineering (EER), Chemistry (CER), Geoscience (GER), and related fields — from across Upstate New York for two days at Cornell University (June 11–12, 2026). The animating question: what could this region’s DBER community build together that no single institution or field could build alone?

The conference was designed as a four-phase consensus-building process:

Phase When Focus
Before Pre-conference survey (53 responses) Hopes for the conference; top barriers & enablers to InterDBER collaboration
During Working group documents (9 small groups, both days) Naming specific barriers, bright spots, design principles, and draft InterDBER research questions
Right after Post-conference survey (21 responses) Conference evaluation, concrete follow-up plans, and commitments
Follow-up Card sort / Delphi rating round (12 invited, 8–10 responses per item) Community rating of each barrier’s severity & changeability, each enabler’s potential & feasibility, and prioritization of collaboration types and research topics

This report synthesizes all four phases. Barriers and enablers are presented close to each group’s original language in Sections 4–5, and Section 5.3 (barriers) and Section 4.3 (enablers) now report the results of the follow-up community rating round described above — completed after the conference, closing the loop the working groups started.

All individual quotes and comments below are anonymized and presented as themes, not attributed to named participants.

1. Who Was in the Room

Nine small groups met throughout the conference (rotating between Working Group 1, Working Group 2, and the closing visioning session), each with 4–6 participants spanning multiple institutions, DBER fields, and career stages — from graduate students to senior faculty, across R1 universities, primarily-undergraduate institutions, and community colleges.

2. What People Came Hoping For

Pre-conference, participants described what they most hoped to get out of the conference and what they were bringing to share. Common threads:

  • Finding collaborators with complementary skills or shared interests — a recurring “who should I be looking for” theme, often phrased as wanting someone from a specific institution type (community college, R1) or with specific methodological expertise.
  • Learning how other DBER fields approach shared problems — assessment, AI in the classroom, and retention/belonging came up across many responses.
  • Bringing something concrete to the table — datasets, methods expertise, or lived experience navigating a specific institutional barrier.

3. Poster Session Gallery

Two poster sessions ran across four tracks: AI & Technology, Pedagogy & Assessment, Equity, Identity & Belonging, and Careers, Research Experiences & Curriculum/Community. Presenters gave 30-second lightning talks before each session opened, and attendees were asked to visit at least one poster from their own DBER field and one from another.

(Poster images are AI-generated conference visuals summarizing the poster session; see the conference program for the full list of presenters and titles.)

Before the conference, participants ranked what makes cross-institutional and InterDBER collaboration work well, from most to least important.

4.2 Working groups: bright spots

During Working Group 2, all nine groups discussed real collaborations that worked and what made them possible. Kept close to each group’s own language:

Cross-cutting themes that came up in multiple groups: clear/explicit communication and norm-setting; a designated convener or logistics lead; shared vision and mutual benefit; capitalizing on existing structures (centers like RIT’s CASTLE, Cornell’s CDER) that already create low-stakes, frequent cross-disciplinary contact; and in-person relationship-building as a precondition for trust.

4.3 Card sort results: which enablers are most feasible and highest-impact?

In the follow-up rating round, participants sorted the consolidated list of enablers twice: once by feasibility (“how realistic is this for the NYDBER community to actually do?”) and once by expected improvement (“how much would this move the needle on InterDBER or inter-institutional collaboration?”). Ten of the twelve invited participants completed this question.

High feasibility AND high impact (the network’s clearest near-term priorities): a shared communication space (Slack) for the network (90% called it feasible, 30% major improvement); existing structures/centers like CASTLE and CDER (80% feasible); and small grants or dedicated funding (90% called this at least moderately feasible, and 80% said it would be a major improvement — the single highest-impact-rated enabler in the set).

High impact but lower feasibility — the harder, structural lifts: institutional norms and incentives that reward interdisciplinary work (70% said “not at all feasible” under current conditions, yet 40% still called it a major improvement) and shared vision/mutual benefit (70% major improvement, but only 30% feasible as something the network can directly manufacture).

5.2 Working groups: named barriers

Each Working Group 2 table named specific barriers and sorted them as local vs. systemic and movable vs. hard to change. This table is presented close to verbatim group language and was the starting list for the post-conference severity × changeability rating round described in the conference design (results now reported in Section 5.3 below).

Note on Group 5: this table reported that “almost all our barriers are systemic” without naming individual items in the structured table — a useful data point in itself about how that group perceived the landscape.

Barrier landscape at a glance

5.3 Card sort results: severity × changeability

This is the follow-up round the conference design called for. After the conference, all participants were invited back to rate the consolidated barrier list on changeability (sorted into “Not addressable at all” / “Moderate” / “Addressable”) and on impediment severity (sorted into “No impediment” / “Moderate” / “Major impediment”). Twelve people were invited; 10 rated any given barrier.

A methodology note on reading this data: this was a drag-and-drop card sort, not a 1–5 Likert scale, so “percent” below means the share of respondents who placed that item in this specific bucket, out of the ~10 who sorted it at all — not out of all 12 survey invitees, and a handful of items with less crisp underlying chart data are flagged approximate in the source file (data/card_sort_barriers.csv) rather than presented as exact.

Highest priority (severe AND hard to change) — the structural core: the federal funding landscape was the single starkest result in the whole rating round: every respondent who sorted it called it “not addressable at all,” and 70% called it a major impediment. Time, workload, and motivation constraints followed the same pattern (70% major impediment, only 10% called it addressable). Differing promotion & tenure/graduation requirements was judged almost universally hard to change (90% not addressable) with real but more moderate severity (30% major impediment).

Severe but more addressable — the best return on effort: lack of awareness of/networks with other DBER researchers, especially for students and postdocs, stood out as both a real impediment (50% major impediment) and the most fixable barrier in the whole list (90% called it addressable). This is arguably the clearest “start here” item for the network.

Named but judged lower-priority: field-specific jargon and credit/authorship negotiation were both rated addressable by large majorities (50% and 90%) and low-impediment by most respondents — real, but not where the community’s effort is most needed right now.

6. Design Principles for Going Forward

Each Working Group 2 table proposed 1–4 design principles for InterDBER collaboration, paired with what each would look like in practice.

Principles that surfaced independently across multiple tables: early-career and community-college inclusion, methodological pluralism, explicit/documented norms for credit and authorship, and building in space for “half-baked ideas” before they’re polished.

7. Draft InterDBER Research Questions

Working Group 1 asked each table to draft 1–3 research topics that genuinely require more than one DBER field to answer well.

Recurring topic clusters: generative AI’s impact on students and pedagogy (named by more tables than any other topic); cross-field workforce/career pathways; how disciplines differ in teaching foundational/shared content; and assessment across disciplinary contexts.

7.1 Card sort results: which research topics should the network prioritize?

The follow-up round asked participants to sort the eight consolidated research topics by feasibility for a regional network to actually pursue, and separately by how much each topic would improve InterDBER or inter-institutional collaboration if pursued. Eight of the twelve invited participants completed this question.

Clearest joint priority: retention, attrition, and sense of belonging across DBER fields was rated feasible by 50% and, notably, 0% said it would produce no improvement — every respondent who sorted it saw at least moderate value. Institutional change and incentive structures was the single highest-impact topic (63% major improvement) despite being middle-of-the-pack on feasibility (38%) — a structural topic in the same spirit as the highest-severity barriers above. Generative AI’s impact on students and learning, despite being the most-named topic during the working groups, drew a genuinely split verdict in the card sort (50% feasible, but also 38% “no improvement”) — worth the network’s attention but not a slam-dunk consensus pick. Universal or cross-field conceptual frameworks was the clearest lower-priority item: half the respondents called it “not at all feasible.”

Research topic card sort results, ranked by expected impact (n=8)
Topic Feasible (%) Not feasible (%) Major improvement (%) No improvement (%)
Institutional change and incentive structures (tenure, credit) across disciplines 38 13 63 13
Generative AI’s impact on students, teaching, and learning across STEM 50 13 38 38
Cross-field workforce and career pathways for STEM students 13 0 38 25
Retention, attrition, and sense of belonging across DBER fields 50 0 25 0
How instruction of foundational/shared content differs by discipline 50 13 25 38
Assessing different types of learning and skills across disciplinary contexts 38 13 25 25
How DBER as a field has changed over time, across disciplines 38 0 25 38
Universal or cross-field conceptual frameworks for describing STEM learning 13 50 13 25

One participant flagged a gap in the topic list itself: “There don’t seem to be as many affective research areas explicitly mentioned” — citing ethics (beyond AI), empathy, and the nature of human-human relations and communication as areas that deserve their own spot rather than folding into the categories above. Worth carrying into the next round of topic-setting.

9. Where This Goes Next

9.1 Sustainability mechanisms people said they’d actually use

Both the post-conference survey (Q24) and the closing-session visioning tables (1–5 enthusiasm ratings per mechanism) asked what would sustain this community. Combining both sources:

Mechanism Times selected (post-survey)
Annual regional symposium 15
Slack workspace for updates and communication 13
Virtual seminar series (e.g., works-in-progress presentations) 12
Shared graduate student training or mentoring program 12
Cross-institutional reading or writing group (monthly, virtual) 9
Shared repository of instruments, protocols, and resources 8
Listserv / email list 7
Job and opportunity sharing (postings, dissertation defenses, etc.) 6
Writing retreats (in-person or virtual) 6
Network newsletter or blog for sharing works-in-progress 4
Other: 2

Highest and most consistent enthusiasm: annual regional symposium, “share and learn” seminars, and research exchange opportunities. Most divided: a network newsletter/blog and a shared digital repository — both drew high interest from some tables and low interest from others, usually tied to who would maintain them.

9.1.1 Card sort results: feasibility and impact of specific mechanisms

The follow-up round asked participants to sort a longer, more granular list of possible collaboration mechanisms — the same ones summarized above, broken out individually — by feasibility and by expected improvement to InterDBER collaboration. Nine of twelve invited participants completed this question.

The clearest “just do this” mechanisms — near-unanimous on both feasibility and impact: a Slack workspace (100% feasible) and listserv/email list (100% feasible) were the only two mechanisms every respondent called fully feasible, though neither drew a majority “major improvement” rating — these read as necessary infrastructure rather than transformative on their own. Job and opportunity sharing was similarly near-unanimous on feasibility (100%) and drew the strongest impact rating of the “just build it” tier (67% major improvement).

Highest expected impact overall: the annual regional symposium — already the front-runner in the closing-session enthusiasm ratings above — was rated a major improvement by 89% of card-sort respondents, the single highest score of any mechanism in the entire round, despite only 22% calling it fully “feasible” outright (most placed it in “moderate” feasibility, consistent with the real logistical lift of running a recurring in-person event). Graduate student seminar exchanges showed a similar profile: high expected impact (67% major improvement) paired with moderate-not-slam-dunk feasibility.

9.2 Three-month commitments

Participants committed to concrete next steps. Common patterns across the closing-session commitments and post-survey Q25 responses:

  • Starting or joining a journal club at their home institution
  • Connecting other DBER researchers at their institution to the network
  • Following up directly with specific people met at the conference
  • Advocating for the network with their institution’s leadership

Appendix: Data Notes

  • Pre-conference survey: 53 total responses (41 completed).
  • Post-conference survey: 21 total responses (19 completed).
  • Working group data drawn from 9 filled tables each for Working Group 1 (InterDBER research topics) and Working Group 2 (barriers, enablers, design principles), plus 9 closing-session visioning tables (sustainability ratings and commitments). A small number of tables did not fill in every field; those are reflected as gaps rather than inferred.
  • Card sort / Delphi rating round: conducted after the conference as a follow-up to the working-group sessions, using a drag-and-drop “group items into buckets” question format in Qualtrics rather than a numeric Likert scale. 12 participants were invited; the number who rated any given item ranged from 8 (research topics) to 10 (barriers and enablers) to 9 (collaboration mechanisms) — not everyone answered every question. Reported percentages are the share of respondents who placed a given item somewhere in that question who put it in the specific bucket named — see Sections 4.3, 5.3, 7.1, and 9.1.1. A handful of individual values in data/card_sort_barriers.csv are marked approximate where the underlying chart rendering made an exact count harder to confirm; these did not change the overall ranking of priorities.
  • All quotes and group notes are anonymized to theme-level or group-level attribution per project guidance; no individual names appear in this report.
  • Structured source data for every table in this report lives in data/ alongside this .Rmd file, so figures and tables can be re-run or extended directly.
